\title{Orbital Periods for K2 Single-transit and Single-eclipse Events from K2 Revisits and TESS}

\author[orcid=0009-0000-7524-4470]{Jon McBee}
\affiliation{Independent researcher, USA}
\email{jon.mcbee@gmail.com}

\begin{abstract}
\citet{LaCourse2018} catalogued 164 K2 events seen only once. We searched all later K2 campaigns
and all TESS data for repeats of the 144 events that TESS should detect. Every period we report
comes from fitted eclipse times and was re-derived blind with independent code. We link K2 C5
and C16 transits to the TESS transits of TOI-5560.01, narrowing its period from $\leq702$\,d to
$140.4939$ or $70.2470$\,d. The K2 planet candidate EPIC~211503363 has $P=122.905$ or
$61.453$\,d, but its companion is $\approx2.2\,R_{\rm J}$, probably an M dwarf. We give new or
refined periods or short alias lists for nine eclipsing binaries. These include HD~220967, a
bright, eccentric ($e\geq0.58$), 73.245-d system. In another, EPIC~202126877, the primary eclipse
deepened from 6\% in 2014 to 20\% in 2021 and 32\% in 2025.
\end{abstract}

\keywords{\uat{Exoplanet detection methods}{489} --- \uat{Transit photometry}{1709} --- \uat{Eclipsing binary stars}{444}}

\section{Sample and Methods}

The catalogue lists 164 events on 163 stars. We kept the 144 events that have TESS coverage, an
expected TESS signal-to-noise ratio of at least 7 per event, and a physical depth. For each
star we combined K2 PDCSAP light curves from every campaign \citep{Howell2014} with TESS SPOC,
TESS-SPOC \citep{Caldwell2020} and QLP \citep{Huang2020} light curves. For recent sectors
without pipeline products we added our own TESScut photometry \citep{Brasseur2019}.

A box of the catalogued depth and duration was slid along the data. A repeat needs SNR $\geq8$,
a depth of 0.5--2 times the catalogued value, and at least 80\% coverage. Periods were then
tested against every predicted epoch, and a period is rejected if one falls on flat data. The
red-noise factor is measured on a baseline of at least twice the duration, so long eclipses on
giants are not misjudged. For eccentric binaries, primary and secondary eclipses were assigned
jointly, and every predicted eclipse in the data had to be seen.

Final periods come from trapezoid fits to each eclipse and a linear ephemeris. Three blind
analyses with independent code, starting from the catalogue epoch alone, re-derived every period
in Table~\ref{tab:k2}. Apart from EPIC~202126877, which shows timing variations, they agree with
ours within $2\sigma$. An adversarial review found pipeline problems that we fixed before the
final run. As a validation, Sanders~617
in M67 comes out at $62.59466\pm0.00018$\,d. \citet{Sandquist2021} give
$62.59484\pm0.00003$\,d.

Before claiming a period, we checked each star against ExoFOP, VizieR (including VSX), SIMBAD, the
Villanova K2 EB catalogue and Gaia DR3 \citep{Gaia2023,Arenou2023}.

\section{Results}

Of the 144 events, 62 show at least one candidate repeat, and 16 have a period that explains two
or more. Of these, 14 are in Table~\ref{tab:k2}. EPIC~202137580 is already well catalogued, and
the giant EPIC~212694013 keeps over ten aliases ($973.79/N$\,d). A fifteenth system, HD~220967, has
primary and secondary eclipses of similar depth that no single period fits; a joint ephemeris
resolves it. Events with a single repeat were not vetted systematically, so the table is not
complete.

\textit{TOI-5560.01 (EPIC~211924561).} SPOC alerted this candidate from a single transit in
Sector 46; after a second in Sector 72, the maximum period was 702.47\,d. The K2 C5 transit and a
C16 transit fit one linear ephemeris with the TESS pair. The C16 transit is masked in the EVEREST
and K2SFF products but clear in K2 PDCSAP and raw SAP data. The cycle counts (7, 17, 22) share no
common factor, and flat data exclude every shorter period except half. This gives
$P=140.49392\pm0.00014$ or $70.24696\pm0.00007$\,d, with
$T_0={\rm BJD_{TDB}}\,2457179.8979\pm0.0014$. The transit is V-shaped ($\approx2.3$\,ppt,
3.0\,h) and far shorter than a central transit across this F star (12--15\,h), so the orbit is
grazing, eccentric, or both. Gaia DR3 epoch radial velocities are not variable
($p=0.08$, 22 transits). Their scatter implies $M_2\sin i\lesssim0.1\,M_\odot$ for a circular
orbit. Both periods predict a transit at ${\rm BJD_{TDB}}\,2461394.716\pm0.004$ (2026 December
20, 05:03\,UTC). A transit at 2461464.963 (2027 February 28) would confirm 70.25\,d. The 100-d
placeholder period in the Villanova catalogue and a 31.27-d SPOC TCE \citep{Valizadegan2025} are
both excluded by the four transits.

\textit{EPIC~211503363.} This single-transit planet candidate of \citet{Kovacs2020} transits
again in Sectors 45 and 72 (3.4--3.8\,ppt, 23\,h). This leaves $P=122.9052\pm0.0006$ or
$61.4526\pm0.0003$\,d; the detrended QLP flux removes both TESS events, but QLP SAP flux and our
own photometry show them. Its host is evolved: Gaia DR3 gives $R_\star=3.6\,R_\odot$ and
$\log g=3.46$. The companion is therefore $\approx2.1$--$2.4\,R_{\rm J}$. That is larger than a
planet or brown dwarf on a non-irradiated orbit, and matches an M dwarf. \citet{Kovacs2020}
lists $R_p=0.260$ in a column labelled Jupiter radii, but $\sqrt{0.004019}\times4.098\,R_\odot
=0.260\,R_\odot$ ($2.5\,R_{\rm J}$), so the value is in solar radii. His BLS period of 73.91\,d is
a formal value close to the data span, not one of our aliases.

\textit{Eclipsing binaries.} HD~220967 ($G=9.4$, F7/8\,V) shows two eclipse types, 37\% and 30\%
deep, in K2 C12 and TESS. The secondary falls at phase 0.867, so $e\cos\omega\approx0.59$ and
$e\geq0.58$. It lasts 1.9 times as long as the primary, which suggests $e\approx0.66$. It is a
bright, long-period benchmark for spectroscopy. For EPIC~211892898, a red giant, the eclipse
ephemeris matches the Gaia DR3 SB1 orbit ($72.53\pm0.03$\,d). The eclipses fall at the predicted primary
conjunctions within $1.8\sigma$. \citet{Libralato2016} had noted its eclipses. For EPIC~211489484
our ephemeris excludes the 106.94-d period of a SPOC TCE \citep{Valizadegan2025}.

EPIC~202126877 is a known 21.78-d EB \citep{IJspeert2024}, but the K2 data change the picture.
The K2 eclipse lies on cycle $-124$ of the TESS-only ephemeris, 2\,h early, consistent with the
eclipse-timing scatter of 10--25\,min seen in TESS. It is only 6.2\% deep in both EVEREST and
K2SFF, and K2 shows no secondary ($<0.1\%$). In our own TESS photometry with a
fixed aperture, the primary is 20\% deep in 2021, 26\% in 2023 and 32\% in 2025. Over the same
time the secondary grows from 4\% to 11\%. Dilution cannot change the secondary-to-primary ratio
(0.21 to 0.43), and the K2 aperture is uncrowded (CROWDSAP 0.999). A precessing orbit, perhaps
driven by a third body, is a plausible cause.

For the C0 binaries, our 34.7456-d period for EPIC~202072917 agrees with the QLP period of
\citet{IJspeert2024} and a SPOC TCE \citep{Valizadegan2025}. Our 22.9041-d period for
EPIC~202071902 agrees with \citet{Guo2025} and is 0.045\,d ($3\sigma$) from the SB2 period of
\citet{Kovalev2024}. Their VSX periods (3.842 and 8.697\,d) come from a machine-learning
classification \citep{Armstrong2016}. Those periods would put several eclipses in every TESS
sector, which is not seen.

\section{Conclusion}

K2 revisits and TESS turn many K2 single events into periods. Most are eclipsing binaries, but the
search also narrows a TESS planet candidate to two periods and identifies a K2 planet candidate as
a probable M dwarf. Code, fits and all three blind analyses are at
\url{https://github.com/coracle-us/duo-transits}.
